quote: Looks like we just need a utility bill and a time to come by and show you a solar design. Is that right?
stewart_read: This is framed as an in-person visit ('come by') on a prior-contact/recycled-style lead rather than a standard phone-appointment setter call, which explains why several button_up elements (phone appointment specified, no-driving/computer instruction) don't appear later — those elements are built for phone closer appointments and may not apply to an in-person format.
coaching_implication: Manager should confirm with the rep whether this account type genuinely uses an in-person visit format; if so, script_coverage gaps on phone-specific button-up items are structurally expected rather than a rep failure, and coaching should focus on the in-person-appropriate equivalents (confirm access, confirm who will be home, confirm bill in hand).

quote: How long is the warranty? Because my roof has a lifetime warranty.
stewart_read: Rep answers a direct product-comparison question with a specific figure (25 years) instead of using the universal escape hatch to route this to the closer, getting pulled deeper into a debate he's not equipped to fully resolve.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep could be reading this as a quick factual answer rather than scope creep since it's a single number, not a sustained technical explanation — but the follow-up hedge ('But, I mean, it sounds like we should be good') shows the rep talking himself into a conclusion rather than redirecting.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to use the escape hatch here: 'That's exactly the kind of comparison our specialist will walk through with you side-by-side' rather than offering his own read on whether the two warranties stack up favorably.

quote: We can we can run a report for your home and show you a quote because we'd be able to tell exactly how much sunlight you are getting and if it would be worth it to do it
stewart_read: This is a clean strategy match for the schema's redirect-to-design pattern: instead of debating sun exposure in the abstract, the rep offers the data-driven report as the path to a real answer. This is the call's best moment and should be reinforced, not flagged as a miss.
coaching_implication: Point to this exact line as the model for how to handle viability doubts — redirect to design rather than reassure with guesses.

quote: We just wanna see if we can can help you cut down on costs or whatever your main motive in wanting to go solar is.
stewart_read: The Verify beat 'What interested you in solar?' is never genuinely asked anywhere in the call — this line is a hedge inside a reassurance sentence, not a direct question to Carl, so his actual motive for going solar is never captured.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to explicitly ask 'what got you interested in looking at solar in the first place?' early in the call — with a customer already voicing doubts, anchoring to his stated motive would give the rep something concrete to tie the appointment to instead of relying on generic cost-cutting language.

quote: I I don't get a lot of sun. The more more I thought about it, I have the limited, amount of sun that gets on my roof.
stewart_read: This is a viability/skepticism objection where the rep does eventually redirect well (01:56), but there's no acknowledgment of the underlying bill-pain motive that might counter the sun objection emotionally before pivoting to the data offer.
alternative_hypothesis: The redirect-to-design move at 01:56 may be sufficient on its own without an emotional flip, since the schema explicitly endorses redirect-to-design as valid strategy for this type of objection — this entry exists to flag the missed emotional layer, not to fault the redirect itself.
coaching_implication: The redirect was good; the additional opportunity is to pair it with a quick bill-pain question first ('what's driving you to look at solar despite the sun concern?') to build a stronger case for keeping the appointment.

stewart_read: The date-negotiation sequence moves quickly through several rejected days without ever running the full button-up sequence (hour block, no-driving/computer instruction, is-that-fair handshake) once Saturday is locked in.
coaching_implication: Even in a compressed or in-person-style call, the rep should still confirm the appointment length and get a verbal 'does that work for you' commitment rather than moving straight into wrap-up pleasantries.

quote: Yeah. I just okay. Let me send in my, my utility bill with the the graph on it.
stewart_read: Customer agrees to send the bill but it is never actually sent during the call — this is a promise-to-send, not a captured bill, and the appointment is booked before that promise is fulfilled.
coaching_implication: Flag this appointment as bill-pending in the handoff — closer should know the design may need to be finalized once the bill photo/email actually arrives.

quote: I I just don't wanna send you guys on a wild goose chase because, you know, I I think it's gonna be very limited in what we can do.
stewart_read: The customer books the Saturday appointment while explicitly pre-framing it as likely a waste of everyone's time. The rep never revisits or neutralizes this framing after it's said, leaving it hanging into the booking.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: rep may have judged that pushing further on this line would re-open the objection rather than close it, and chose to let the comment pass and move toward locking a date instead — supported by the rep immediately pivoting to reassurance about volume of appointments (02:42) rather than debating the point further.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to close the loop verbally before locking a date: 'Even if it turns out limited, would it help to at least see the real numbers so you know for sure?' turns the hedge into a small commitment rather than leaving it unaddressed.
